title: Real exchange rates in the European price revolution
Conceptual divergence analysis: LLM-assisted mapping of a researcher’s conceptual vocabulary against their curated literature
abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM)-based research tools often overlook a researcher-specific problem in manuscript writing: where does my use of a key theoretical term stand relative to the literature I want to address? We introduce Conceptual Divergence Analysis (CDA), an LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation pipeline to compare theoretical term usage in a researcher’s manuscripts with usage in a researcher-curated literature corpus. We propose reflective calibration as the individual-level scientometric function this workflow performs. We demonstrate CDA on two research programs, encompassing corpora of roughly 3,200 and 2,800 papers and four theoretical terms. The analyses reveal researcher-specific divergences consequential for theoretical positioning. In one case, the researcher draws a distinction the literature leaves underarticulated. In another case, CDA reveals how a term carries different meanings across disciplinary traditions, helping the researcher anticipate how different scholarly audiences may interpret its use. Register assignments are anchored to pre-computed clusters. An optional researcher-led validation step records the researcher’s judgment before revealing the model’s interpretation, making agreement or disagreement explicit. We release the complete pipeline as an open-source resource with a no-installation hosted demonstration on a public toy corpus, extending an individual-level tradition in scientometrics from citation structure to conceptual vocabulary.

title: Financial Constraints, Wages, and Macroeconomic Implications
authors: HAMZEH ARABZADEH; ALMUT BALLEER; BRITTA GEHRKE
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how firm‐level financial constraints affect individual wages and aggregate labor market dynamics during financial recessions. We derive testable predictions from competing theoretical mechanisms and assess them empirically using German administrative worker data matched to firm balance sheets. Embedding these microlevel estimates in a macroeconomic model with labor and financial frictions, we demonstrate how small ceteris paribus effects align with large aggregate dynamics. Tighter financial conditions amplify wage and unemployment volatility, weakening the tight link between wage rigidity and the volatility of unemployment discussed in the literature. Financial constraints reduce the effectiveness of hiring subsidies during recessions.
